claims.text: In Trunk's merge queue simulation, increasing batch size from 1 to 16 (logical conflict rate 0.1%) made PRs merge 54.9% slower, from 41m 56s to 1h 5m.
In Trunk's simulation, increasing batch size from 1 to 16 (logical conflict rate 0.1%) cut average CI time per PR by 77.5%, from 41m 28s to 9m 19s.
Trunk's SimMergeQueue ran 8 scenarios: batch sizes 1, 4, 8 and 16, each at logical conflict rates of 0.1% (1/1000) and 0.2% (1/500), with parallel queues for batch sizes above 1.
In Trunk's simulation, the lowest peak CI concurrency occurred at batch size 16 with a 0.1% logical conflict rate, meaning fewer CI runners are needed.
In Trunk's simulation, a higher logical conflict rate (0.2% vs 0.1%) did not significantly change time to merge or CI time per PR.
Time to reject PRs with logical conflicts or flaky tests grows with batch size in Trunk's simulation, because failing batches must be bisected.
Anthropic's CPO Mike Krieger said Anthropic's merge queue became a bottleneck and had to be completely re-architected because agent-written code produced many more pull requests than expected.
Trunk notes parallel queues are only an option when a build system like Bazel is used in the repo.
Graphite reports Parallel CI customers saw 1.5x faster merges overall (33% decrease at p95, 26% at p75), and up to 2.5x faster for heavy stacked-PR users (60% decrease at p95, 34% at p75).

Graphite's Parallel CI uses speculative execution: for stacks A, B, C it tests A, A←B and A←B←C simultaneously; if a stack fails it is evicted and the dependent speculative runs are canceled and restarted.
Graphite's parallel CI only generates extra CI runs when CI fails in the queue, so flaky tests raise cost because the failing PR is evicted and all subsequent speculative runs restart.

Graphite's merge queue treats a stack as the atomic unit; a failure in any PR fails the whole stack. Parallel CI can run on every PR in the stack (strongest guarantee) or only the topmost PR (fewer CI runs).
Graphite recommends setting parallel CI concurrency to match peak PR volume times CI duration, e.g. 3 concurrent runs for 30-minute CI and 3 PRs per 30 minutes at peak.
Graphite's batching (private beta) handles failures either by full parallel isolation (default, faster identification) or bisection (fewer CI runs).

Mergify's parallel checks build temporary batch PRs representing cumulative merges (PR1, PR1+PR2, ...), run CI on them in parallel, and on failure remove the culprit PR; concurrency is set via merge_queue.max_parallel_checks.

Mergify's 'RCV theorem' states a merge queue can optimize only two of reliability, cost and velocity: parallel checks give reliability+velocity with wasted CI on failures, sequential gives reliability+cost with throughput capped at one PR per CI run, batch mode gives velocity+cost but hidden failures can reach main.
Aviator's default sequential mode merges one PR per full CI suite duration; with 30-minute CI the maximum is 48 PRs per day.

Aviator's parallel mode creates bot PRs containing each PR plus all PRs ahead in the queue; if an earlier bot PR fails, a queue reset forces revalidation of all subsequent PRs, potentially wasting CI.
Mergify's analysis of 200,000+ merges across 477 teams found the rate of green PRs breaking main rose from 0.77% at 2–5 engineers to 12.5% (1 in 8) at 40+ engineers.

Mergify found AI-assisted PRs broke main 1.9% of the time versus 4.4% for non-AI PRs, holding within repos and PR-size bands; the finding is observational and AI is detected only via commit signatures.

Mergify reports 94% of private merges still go one PR at a time; batches average about four PRs, and failed private batches bundle about 5.8 PRs. Autonomous agent-authored PRs were only a few hundred of 153,000 merges.

GitHub's merge queue shipped 30,000+ PRs with 4.5 million CI runs for GitHub.com before general availability, and now lets GitHub deploy 30+ changes at once versus a 15 limit with the old trains system.
At GitHub, over 500 engineers merge 2,500 PRs per month into the monorepo via merge queue, and average wait time to ship fell by 33%.
Reason Machines' merges went from about 17 to over 600 per day in six weeks with coding agents; on October 12, 84 PRs waited at once and the slowest 5% waited 2.5 hours.

With Mergify tuned to test up to 12 PRs in parallel, the median merge took 3.4 minutes with only 79 seconds being CI; 37 seconds went to detecting readiness, 26 seconds to creating the test branch and draft PR, and about 30 seconds to merging.
